title: DECONSTRUCTED: How David Blough is REBUILDING Commanders Offense by Putting His Players First
text: David Blow isn't just remodeling the offense. He's completely deconstructed it so they can rebuild it as a unit. >> You are Locked On [music] Commanders, your daily podcast on the Washington Commanders, part of the Locked On Podcast Network, your team every day. >> Welcome inside today's episode of Locked On Commanders. I'm your host, your guy on the ground, David Harrison. And on today's episode, practice notes from the second OTA practice open to the media here in Ashburn, Virginia. But first, we're going to start it all off with David Blow talking about not just rebuilding or remodeling this Washington Commanders offense, but really just deconstructing it, really building it entirely from the ground up. And it's something that we actually heard from or heard about from rookie or rookie wide receiver Jaylen Lane last week after the first OTA practice that we were able to attend. And the first OTA practice just altogether. Jaylen Lane really kind of talked about building this thing from the ground up. Has really given the players a unique vision on how it's been built and really kind of a sense of ownership over how it's being built and all these other things. And David Blow, the first time talking to us here this OTA period, this phase three of the offseason program, really kind of talked about that. That was my biggest takeaway from his first press conference here in this phase three is the collaborative effort, the player ownership into the scheme rather than coming through with kind of his system, his way of doing it and saying, you know, this is the way the coach wants you to do it, so this is the way you're going to do it. And I really like the way that he's taken this approach to building this offense around the players. Because if you're going to build it around the players, why not build it for the players? And it's something that we've heard time and time again from coaches across the league, across games, across sports, across whatever uh league you're in. Doesn't matter if it's college, high school, little league, college football, uh NFL football, you hear coaches all the time talk about, "My job is to put the players in the best position to be a or best position to be successful. Yet time and time again, we see coaching staffs fail to do that and they end up collapsing because of it. No guarantee that it's going to go great in Super Bowls and all this other stuff doing it the other way because you can still definitely fail doing it the other way. But to me uh and and to I think a lot of people who listen to this program, that is really kind of the optimal way uh to do it instead of leaning on {quote} we've always done it that way. David Blough and the offensive staff really did spend the off season deconstructing all the concepts, all of the the paces, all of the under center versus shotgun, the wide zone versus all like just anything you think of in an NFL offense, really took the time to deconstruct it, strip it all down so they can really start kind of building it up into a multiple high-tempo, high-variable offense uh that's going to be unique to this 2026 roster. And I think really if you start that way, you kind of do the same thing every off season, uh especially if you have some success, and you come out every single year and the offense is just going to be a little bit different, which is reminiscent we talked about the Brian Flores defense and how people always say, "Well, there's this Brian Flores defense." But one year Brian Flores defense will sport uh five men up front for a majority of the time. The next year it might be four men up front. The next year it might be three men up front. Like the Brian Flores defense really stylistically stays the same, but how it's constructed, how it aligns, how it executes is very different. Sounds like David Blough is kind of going for a similar type of thing. And really he kind of simpli- fied it, right? Said very, very specifically it would be {quote} foolish to dictate exactly how things are going to be run without using the wisdom of his own players. The guy who's going to do it. And this is I think the benefit of having a guy who came up through the ranks, came up through, you know, the NFL rosters, battled for his roster spot, got got to start in the NFL, hasn't forgotten where he's come from. And unfortunately sometimes leaders in all walks of life do forget that times where they came from. David Blough not forgetting where he came from. He's been that quarterback. I don't know where, I'm not going to accuse anybody of anything, but he's been that quarterback. Sat in a room and probably like, you know, like this just isn't really kind of the offense that like this running back doesn't really like to do these types of runs. He's really isn't really great at them. This receiver isn't really great at these types of routes. I'm not really great at this type of throw. Yet, the offensive coordinator, head coach, whoever was like, "Hey, this is the offense that I run. You're going to run my offense. Do what I do." He hasn't forgotten the the the background. And with Jayden Daniels coming in, shifting to that collaborative effort, we heard Jayden Daniels speak last week about really helping to build this thing as a group. And I told you guys here every day, as you remember, it reminded me of when Drew Brees went to New Orleans with Sean Payton, and they did the same thing. Stripped it down to the nuts and bolts, rebuilt this thing up from the frame into an offense they both wanted, and expanding some of the things they were doing. So, it's not just doing what Jayden's comfortable with. That's where it kind of sounds a little bit different. It's not just let's do what Jayden's already comfortable with. No, it's let's do what Jayden's comfortable with, but let's also find the ways to use what you're good at and expand your skills. Going under center, mastering those play-action concepts, stretching defenses both horizontally and vertically. It's a work in progress. It's something that's going to take a lot of effort. You see moments out here on the practice field where it just clicks, and it looks good, and it looks second nature. You're just like, "Man, I can't believe they weren't always doing this." But, you're adding these wrinkles because it's something that Jayden's good at. And certainly, there are times where you do see that this is a unit that's in progress. It's a system that's in progress, and learning curves, and growing pains, uh things like that. But, those are to be expected. They're not discouraging uh because they're happening in early June. Now, we get to like the end of training camp, things are happening. Get to the regular season, things are happening. Uh then maybe it'll be a little bit different. But, of course, uh not happening often enough to be worried about it for one, and two, it's early enough in the process that you're like, "Yeah, there's going to be a a hiccup here or there." If there's like one hiccup a practice, I I think you can live with that. When the offense is fully engaged this fall, what David Blau wants from his unit, we heard Dan Quinn call success from his unit, what David Blau wants from his unit is he wants three non-negotiables. He wants strict ball security, which so far so good. There was one interception on the practice field today. Marcus Mariota threw an interception to Percy Butler. The offense said it was incomplete, the defense said it was complete. It was an interception pretty much as biased as you would expect it to be, but it was miscommunication on a route. Something that they can get cleaned up pretty easily. They want to generate explosive plays. We've definitely seen the opportunity for those explosive plays out here on the practice field just in the two days we've been able to come watch these plays and they want to execute high-level situational football. Two end-of-game scenarios were running today's practice out here during the OTAs. Both times the offense was able to get into range for what would be a potentially game-winning score. Dan Quinn talked about David Blough's collaborative approach again today. Said, "Quote, I would say that's no different than him as an assistant to now. The thing I liked about what I've seen throughout the off season is his collaboration. There's a lot of experience on the staff and so using all that wisdom in different ways, I think that's one of the things that I've been impressed by, but it's his ability to not just connect with the quarterbacks, but with the entire offense as an entire group. title: PROVING GROUNDS: Commanders OTAs a LAUNCH Point for Sam Hartman and Others, to Prove Their Value
text: While he's far from alone, Sam Hartman tops my list of guys with something to prove this offseason. >> You are Locked On Commanders, your daily [music] podcast on the Washington Commanders, part of the Locked On Podcast Network, your team every day. >> Welcome inside today's episode of Locked On Commanders. I'm your host, your guy on the ground, David Harrison. And on today's episode, as we head into OTA practice number two, at least open for the media practice number two, we talk about the latest on a wide receiver a lot of people are expecting to arrive to Washington. The question is, when will he be arriving? We'll also talk about the use of 12 and 13 personal packages and how it might be the savior for a questionable wide receiver room. But we're starting it all off with the guys in on the roster or on the roster, I should say, who have the most to prove during the OTAs, mandatory mini camp, and even heading into training camp. A pretty OTA practice number two mailbag and Robbie came through. Who has a lot to prove during OTAs? And I think that, you know, I generally kind of subscribe to the Jayden Daniels theory of, you know, if you don't come in every single day thinking you've got something to prove, you're probably in the wrong business. I know that that's something that we preach here at the Locked On Network is like every time you turn on this camera, every time you step in front of a mic or behind a mic, and you ask, you know, the audience, you good people, Commanders fans, to dedicate some of your time or to donate some of your time to what we're producing here at the network, you better bring your A game, you better prove it to people that you're worth them giving that time to. So, I like that mentality, I like that approach. And I've got a list of guys who do have some things to prove here this OTA period. Of course, it's going to lead into the mini camp, lead into training camp. Uh but it's going to start off with quarterback Sam Hartman. I think we all basically thought the same thing when quarterback Ethan Kelly-Moore was drafted out of Ruckers in the was drafted out of Rutgers in the Uh that, you know, I I mean, some people even dropped the hammer right there and said, "Well, there goes Sam Hartman." Obviously, you have Jayden Daniels, you've got Marcus Mariota. The Commanders have been a team these last 2 years that have carried three quarterbacks on the active roster so they can take advantage of that emergency quarterback rule, but it's been a veteran. It's been Jeff Driskel. It's been Josh Johnson. You know what I mean? Very rarely has it been a young guy. So, Sam Hartman, now in his third season, just like Jayden Daniels, came in as an undrafted free agent in the same off season. Very good friends, all those types of things. There was even some conversation amongst uh fan groups. I don't know how much the media really got into it, but uh that last year Sam was kept on the practice squad just because he's buddies with Jayden. I don't really think that's the case because I don't think these guys are going to make these decisions for those reasons, but I know that narrative was kind of out there a little bit, but the drafting of Ethan Caliakman, it's look, it did it signal something to Sam Hartman, which was, "Listen, we're not 100% set that you are our young backup quarterback uh of the future. So, to go get another guy who could potentially be that third quarterback and could potentially even grow into becoming the second quarterback. And before you even talk about either of these guys becoming the second quarterback, I think that's where the battle is is for that third quarterback spot. So, Sam Hartman, even just in that light, definitely has something to prove. Next guy on my list, I think is offensive lineman Brandon Coleman. And to be completely straight up about this list, this is not in any type of like uh you know, most to prove. I think like I said, Sam Hartman is the top guy on my list.
